'''''Rosa'' × ''centifolia''''' (lit. hundred leaved rose; syn. ''R. gallica'' var. ''centifolia'' (L.) Regel), the '''Provence rose''', '''cabbage rose''', '''May rose''' or '''Rose de Mai''', is a [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] [[rose]] developed by Dutch breeders in the period between the 17th century and the 19th century, possibly earlier.

==History==
Its parentage includes [[Rosa × damascena|''Rosa'' × ''damascena'']], but it may be a complex hybrid; its exact hereditary history is not well documented or fully investigated,<ref name=P&R>{{cite book |author1=Phillips, R. |author2=Rix, M. |year=2004 |title=The Ultimate Guide to Roses: A Comprehensive Selection |publisher=Macmillan |isbn=1-4050-4920-0 }}</ref> but it now appears that this is not the "hundred-leaved" (''centifolia'') rose mentioned by [[Theophrastus]] and [[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]]: "no unmistakable reference can be traced earlier than about 1580".<ref>Alice M. Coats ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'', (1964) 1992, p. 175.</ref>

The original plant was sterile, but a [[sport (biology)|sport]] with single flowers appeared in 1769, from which various cultivars known as '''centifolia roses''' were developed, many of which are further hybrids.<ref name=P&R/> Other cultivars have appeared as further sports from these roses. ''Rosa'' × ''centifolia'' 'Muscosa' is a sport with a thick covering of resinous hairs on the flower buds, from which most (but not all) "'''moss roses'''" are derived. Dwarf or miniature sports have been known for almost as long as the larger forms, including a miniature moss rose 'Moss de Meaux'.

In 1783 the French artist [[Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun]] painted a [[Marie Antoinette with a Rose|famous portrait of Marie Antoinette holding a pink centifolia rose]].

==Growth==
Individual plants are shrubby in appearance, growing to 1.5–2 m tall, with long drooping canes and greyish green pinnate leaves with 5–7 leaflets. The flowers are round and globular, with numerous thin overlapping petals that are highly scented; they are usually pink, less often white to dark red-purple.

==Cultivation and uses==
''R.'' × ''centifolia'' is particular{{Clarify|date=March 2013}} to the French city of [[Grasse]], known as the perfume capital of the world. It is widely cultivated for its singular fragrance — clear and sweet, with light notes of honey. The flowers are commercially harvested for the production of [[rose oil]], which is commonly used in perfumery.

==Centifolia cultivars==
Cultivars of ''Rosa'' × ''centifolia'' that are still grown include:<ref name=P&R/>
* 'Bullata', also called 'Lettuce Rose' and 'À Feuilles de Laitue', known since 1801
* 'Cristata',<ref name = RHSPF1>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/98552/Rosa-x-centifolia-Cristata-(Ce)/Details |title=''Rosa'' × ''centifolia'' 'Cristata' |publisher=RHS |access-date=18 February 2020 }}</ref> also called 'Chapeau de Napoleon'
* 'Fantin-Latour',<ref name = RHSPF2>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/94922/Rosa-Fantin-Latour-(Ce)/Details |title=''Rosa'' × ''centifolia'' 'Fantin Latour |publisher=RHS |access-date=18 February 2020 }}</ref> blush pink, fragrant
* 'Petite de Hollande', also called 'Pompon des Dames', known since the 18th century
* 'Rose de Meaux', also called "Rosa pomponia", known since 1637
* 'Unique Blanche', also called 'Mutabilis', 'White Provence', 'Vièrge de Cléry' and other names
* 'Village Maid', introduced by Vibert in 1845, a striped flower

Both 'Centifola'<ref name = RHSPF1/> and 'Fantin-Latour'<ref name = RHSPF2/> are recipients of the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].
